questions.prompt: To decide in O(n) whether an array contains any duplicate, the standard approach is to:

options.text: Compare every pair of elements
Sort the array and scan
Use binary search for each element
Insert elements into a hash set and report a duplicate on the first collision

questions.explanation: A hash set gives O(1) average membership tests, so one pass detects a repeat. Sorting first works but costs O(n log n); pairwise comparison is O(n^2).

questions.prompt: The two-sum problem (find indices of two numbers adding to a target) is solved in O(n) using:

options.text: Sorting then binary search
A hash map storing each value's index, checking for the complement
A min-heap
A nested loop over all pairs

questions.explanation: For each element, look up target minus that element in the map; a hit gives the pair. The single pass with O(1) lookups makes it linear.

questions.prompt: To find the length of the longest consecutive run of integers in an unsorted array in O(n), you:

options.text: Put all values in a hash set and expand each run only from its smallest element
Use a segment tree
Binary search for each value
Sort the array first

questions.explanation: Starting a count only when value - 1 is absent ensures each run is walked once, giving O(n) overall. Sorting would achieve the same result but in O(n log n).

questions.prompt: Grouping a list of words into anagram groups is efficiently done by keying a hash map on:

options.text: The length of each word
The first letter of each word
A random hash
The sorted characters of each word

questions.explanation: Anagrams share the same multiset of letters, so their sorted form is identical and makes a canonical key. A character-count signature works equally well and avoids the sort.

questions.prompt: A frequency map (counting occurrences of each element) is the core of which common task?

options.text: Reversing a linked list
Finding the most frequent element or the top-k frequent elements
Balancing a binary tree
Detecting a cycle in a graph

questions.explanation: Counting into a hash map in O(n), then selecting by count, answers frequency questions directly. Top-k then pairs the map with a heap or bucket sort.

questions.prompt: The set intersection of two arrays is computed efficiently by:

options.text: Comparing every pair across the two arrays
Building a binary search tree of both
Putting one array in a hash set and testing membership of the other's elements
Sorting both and using a heap

questions.explanation: Membership tests against a hash set give O(m + n) total time. Nested comparison is O(mn); sorting both and merging is O(m log m + n log n).

questions.prompt: Why does the count-subarrays-with-sum-k pattern store prefix-sum counts in a hash map?

options.text: So the number of earlier prefixes equal to current sum minus k is available in O(1)
To sort the prefixes
To reverse the array
To detect duplicates in the array

questions.explanation: A subarray sums to k exactly when an earlier prefix equals the current prefix minus k, and the map counts such prefixes instantly. This turns an O(n^2) scan into O(n).

questions.prompt: A hash set is preferred over a sorted structure for membership testing when:

options.text: You need range queries
Order is irrelevant and average O(1) lookups matter most
You need to iterate elements in sorted order
Memory is extremely constrained

questions.explanation: Hashing gives constant-time average membership but no ordering. When ordered iteration or range queries are needed, a balanced tree or sorted array is the right choice despite its O(log n) operations.

questions.prompt: To check whether two strings are anagrams in O(n), you can:

options.text: Build a character-count map for one and decrement it while scanning the other
Compare their lengths only
Sort both and compare, which is optimal
Reverse one and compare

questions.explanation: Counting characters up and down leaves an all-zero map exactly when they are anagrams, in linear time. Sorting also works but costs O(n log n).

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of relying on a hash map's average O(1) guarantee?

options.text: Hash maps cannot store strings
They require sorted input
Adversarial or unlucky keys can cause many collisions, degrading to O(n)
Lookups are always O(log n)

questions.explanation: If many keys collide, chains or probe sequences grow long and operations slow to linear. Randomised hashing defends against adversaries who try to force this worst case.
